title: Flour types and protein content explained
subtitle: Why the protein percentage on the bag determines how your bake behaves
excerpt: Flour protein content determines how much gluten a dough can develop. High-protein strong flours suit bread; low-protein plain flours suit cakes, biscuits, and pastry. The right flour is not interchangeable and understanding why prevents the most common baking failures.
sourceNotes: Flour protein content and its role in baking is well-documented in food science and practical baking literature. Typical protein ranges for UK flours are based on standard industry specifications.

glossaryTerms.definition: The percentage of protein in flour, listed on the packaging nutrition label. Most of this protein is the precursor to gluten. Higher protein means more gluten potential.
All-purpose flour with 9 to 11% protein. The standard for cakes, biscuits, pastry, and sauces. Known as all-purpose flour in the United States.
Bread flour with 12 to 14% protein. The standard for yeasted breads, sourdough, pizza dough, and enriched doughs. Higher protein gives a chewier crumb and stronger gluten network.

content.text: of flour determines how much gluten it can form when mixed with water. Bread needs lots of gluten to trap gas and create a chewy crumb. Pastry and cake need very little gluten, or the result is tough. Using the wrong flour for the job is one of the most common reasons bakes fail.
UK flour types at a glance
Plain flour (all-purpose): 9 to 11% protein. For cakes, biscuits, shortcrust pastry, scones, batter.
Self-raising flour: plain flour with baking powder added, 9 to 11% protein. For sponge cakes and scones where a reliable, measured rise is needed.
Strong white bread flour: 12 to 14% protein. For all yeasted breads, sourdough, pizza, croissants, and enriched doughs such as brioche.
Wholemeal flour: 13 to 14% protein, but the bran cuts gluten strands, reducing effective gluten development. Wholemeal doughs absorb more water and rise more slowly than white doughs.
Spelt, einkorn, emmer: ancient wheat varieties with moderate protein (10 to 12%) but more fragile gluten. Good flavour in bread; requires gentler handling than modern wheat.
Rye flour: low gluten-forming capacity regardless of protein content. Rye breads rely on starches and a sourdough culture for structure.

The protein content is on the nutrition label under protein per 100 g. This is the number to use when comparing flours across brands. A flour labelled strong but showing 10% protein is not strong enough for a yeasted loaf.
